title: At Play on the Far Shore
summary: Dārika is at play in the sky, on the far shore, with emptiness and compassion undivided; he asks what use mantra, tantra and concentration are, makes suffering and happiness one as he enjoys the magic show, and, crying 'king, king, king', says other kings are bound by delusion while he, at Lūyī's feet, has gained the twelve stages. Munidatta reads the sky as the three emptinesses and its far shore as clear light, the line on the magic show as an instruction to enjoy sense objects and senses, and the cries of 'king' as pointing to the poet's own qualities, such as lordship of the body.

lines.gloss: rāga (melodic mode) · Varāḍī (name of the rāga)
of emptiness and compassion (suna-karuṇa + -ri) · undivided, nondifferent (abhinna) · by way of (?) · body-speech-mind (kāya-vāk-citta)
lines.en: Through the [nondifference]{abheda} of [emptiness]{sunyata} and [compassion]{karuna}, in [body, speech and mind]{kaya-vak-citta},

flags.note: bārem̐ is uncertain. It looks like the instrumental of a noun bāra, 'way, manner' (or 'turn, time'); the draft renders the phrase 'through the nondifference'. Munidatta's abhedopacāreṇa, 'by treating as non-different' (cp.34.m2), and the Tibetan line's dbye ba med pas, 'by being undivided', both read it as instrumental. kāabākcia has no case ending: the draft makes it the sphere of Dārika's play in 1b ('in body, speech and mind'), as Munidatta does with his 'purified body, speech and mind' (cp.34.m2); it could also go with abhina ('body, speech and mind undivided').

lines.gloss: plays, revels (vilasati) · Dārika · in the sky (gaaṇa + -ta) · on the far shore (pārima-kula + -em̐)
lines.en: [Dārika]{p-darika} is at [play]{lila} in the [sky]{gagana}, on the [far shore]{para}.

flags.note: gaaṇata pārimakulem̐ is two locatives side by side, 'in the sky, on the far shore'. Munidatta takes the second as 'its far shore', the far shore of the sky (cp.34.m2); the draft keeps the two phrases apart, as the Bengali does.

The Tibetan line differs: rnam par rol pa dA ri ka / pha rol mchog gi 'gram du song, 'Dārika, at play, went to the bank of the supreme far side'. It has no word for the sky, adds 'went' (song), and renders pārima as pha rol mchog, 'the supreme far side', as if reading parama. The draft follows the Bengali.
pārimakulem̐ is rendered as one phrase, 'far shore', marked with para (its listed variant); kula-shore is therefore not marked separately (see termsOmitted).

lines.gloss: mind (that is) the mark of the unmarkable (alakṣa-lakha-cittā) · in great bliss (mahāsuha + -e)
lines.en: With a [mind]{citta} that is the [mark of the unmarkable]{alaksya-laksana}, in [great bliss]{mahasukha},

flags.note: The case and role of cittā are unclear. Read as instrumental: 'with a mind that is the mark of the unmarkable' (the draft); as nominative: 'the mind, the mark of the unmarkable, [plays] in great bliss', as the Tibetan line takes it (mtshan nyid med pa'i mtshan nyid sems / bde ba chen pos rnam par rol); or as an adjective of Dārika in 2b: 'Dārika, whose mind is the mark of the unmarkable'. Munidatta paraphrases: the mind, unmarkable, is marked by non-arising (cp.34.m3).

alakṣalakha is rendered with the glossary's 'mark of the unmarkable'. Munidatta cites only alakha and treats the mind as 'marked' (lakṣyate) (cp.34.m3), which would give 'the mind marked as unmarkable'.
The Tibetan adds 'revels' (rnam par rol) to this line, taking it from 2b, where its own version then lacks it.

lines.gloss: plays, revels (vilasati) · Dārika · in the sky (gaaṇa + -ta) · on the far shore (pārima-kula + -em̐)
lines.en: [Dārika]{p-darika} is at [play]{lila} in the [sky]{gagana}, on the [far shore]{para}.

flags.note: This line repeats 1b word for word, and the English repeats 1b exactly. The Tibetan does not repeat itself: its 2b reads dA ri ka pa nam mkha' la / pha rol mchog gi 'gram du song, 'Dārikapa, in the sky, went to the bank of the supreme far side', with the sky but without the play, which it has moved into 2a.

lines.translit: kinto mante kinto tante kinto re jhāṇabakhāne |
lines.gloss: what to you (kiṃ to) · by mantra · what to you · by tantra · what to you · hey (vocative particle) · by concentration and exposition (jhāṇa-bakhāṇa, dhyāna-vyākhyāna)
lines.en: What use is [mantra]{mantra} to you, what use [tantra]{tantra}, what use, hey, [concentration]{dhyana} and [exposition]{vyakhyana}?

flags.note: jhāṇa is dhyāna, rendered with the glossary's 'concentration' (dhyana), which keeps it apart from bhāvanā, 'meditation'. In this list of ritual and scholastic pursuits 'meditation' would read more naturally; the draft keeps the glossary's word and asks (see questions).

kinto is taken as kiṃ + to, 'what [is it] to you': Munidatta has kiṃ tava, 'what to you' (cp.34.m4), and the Tibetan line has khyod kyi, 'your', with each item. re is a vocative particle, 'hey'; Munidatta expands it as re vaṭa bālayogin, 'hey, lad, novice yogin' (cp.34.m4).

jhāṇabakhāne (dhyāna-vyākhyāna) may be a pair, 'concentration and exposition' (the draft), or one thing, 'expounding concentration', that is, lecturing on meditation. Munidatta's dhyānavyākhyānena allows both (cp.34.m4); the Tibetan comment lists reading, concentration and explanation separately, and the Tibetan line makes 'explain' a verb (bsam gtan ci zhig bshad).

lines.gloss: absorbed in non-abiding great bliss (apaiṭhāna-mahāsuha-līṇa + -e) · hard to discern (durlakṣa) · supreme nirvāṇa (parama-nibāṇa + -em̐)
lines.en: Absorbed in [non-abiding]{apratisthana} [great bliss]{mahasukha}: supreme [nirvāṇa]{nirvana}, [hard to discern]{durlaksa}.

flags.note: The relation of the two halves is unclear, and the draft sets them side by side. The ending -em̐ of nibāṇem̐ could be locative: 'absorbed in non-abiding great bliss, in supreme nirvāṇa, hard to discern'. Munidatta makes nirvāṇa the subject: by the play of non-abiding great bliss your nirvāṇa, hard to discern, is accomplished by the guru's grace (cp.34.m4).

The song has līṇe, 'absorbed, dissolved'; Munidatta's paraphrase has līlayā, 'by the play' (cp.34.m4). The Tibetan line (thim, 'dissolved') and the Tibetan comment (thim pa'i phyir) support līṇe, which the draft follows. The Tibetan line also has rang gnas, 'own place', for apaiṭhāna, 'non-abiding' (see the witness note).

lines.translit: duḥkhem̐ sukhem̐ eku kariā bhuñjai indījānī
lines.gloss: suffering · happiness · one · having made · enjoys, eats (bhuṅkte) · magic show (? indrajāla)
lines.en: Making [suffering and happiness]{duhkha-sukha} one, he enjoys the [magic show]{indrajala}.

flags.note: indījānī is rendered 'magic show', as the glossary files it under indrajala (Sanskrit indrajāla; Old Bengali indiāla in song 30), and the Tibetan line supports this: mig 'phrul dra ba, 'net of magic'. But the long ī and the final -ī are unexpected, and another word may lie behind the form. Munidatta does not cite it; his paraphrase has the enjoyment of sense objects and senses (viṣayendriyopabhoga) in its place (cp.34.m5). The line keeps the magic show and puts his reading in a note; see questions.

bhuñjai is third person, 'enjoys' (also 'eats'; the Tibetan has za bar byed, 'eats'). Its subject is unstated, perhaps Dārika, named in 4b, so the draft supplies 'he'. Munidatta turns the line into an instruction to the novice yogin: having asked the guru, enjoy (kuru) (cp.34.m5).

lines.translit: svaparāpara na cebai dārika saalānuttaramāṇī || dhru ||
lines.gloss: self, other and not-other (sva-para-apara) · not · perceives (cetayati) · Dārika · deeming all unsurpassed (sakala-anuttara-mānin?)
lines.en: [Dārika]{p-darika} does not perceive [self and other]{sva-para} or not-other; he deems all [unsurpassed]{anuttara}.

flags.note: svaparāpara is taken as sva, para and apara: 'self and other, or not-other'. The third member could instead be 'another, further': the Tibetan line has rang gzhan gzhan nyid, 'self, other, otherness', and the Tibetan comment rang dang pha rol dang gzhan, 'self, the other side and another'; or parāpara could be the pair 'far and near'. Munidatta repeats the compound: Dārika does not see the division of self, other and the rest in saṃsāra (cp.34.m5).

saalānuttaramāṇī (perhaps sakala-anuttara-mānin) is uncertain. The draft's 'he deems all unsurpassed' is close to the Tibetan line, ma lus bla na med par shes, 'knows all, without remainder, as unsurpassed'. Alternatives: 'deeming himself unsurpassed among all', or, with Munidatta's paraphrase sakalānuttaraṃ gatvā, 'having gone to the unsurpassed of all' (cp.34.m5).

The Tibetan line has no negative: rang gzhan gzhan nyid dA ri ka / ma lus bla na med par shes. Where the Bengali has na cebai, 'does not perceive', and Munidatta na paśyati, 'does not see' (cp.34.m5), the Tibetan has only shes, 'knows'. The draft follows the Bengali.

lines.translit: rāā rāā rāāre abara rāa moherā bādhā
lines.gloss: king · king · O king (rāā + re) · other · king(s) · of delusion (moha + -erā) · bound (baddha)

flags.note: rāāre is taken as rāā + re, 'O king', with the vocative particle of 3a; Munidatta counts three utterances (uktitraya) (cp.34.m6). The Tibetan's third member is a genitive phrase, nyid kyi rgyal, 'king of [the king] himself', as if reading rāāra, 'of the king'.

abara rāa may be plural, 'other kings' (the draft, following Munidatta's plural: gods, lords of nāgas and the like, cp.34.m6), or singular, 'the other king'. The Tibetan gzhan yang can mean 'others too' or 'moreover'.

lines.gloss: at the feet of Lūipāda (Lūipāa + pae) · Dārika · twelve worlds (dvādaśa-bhuvana + -em̐) · gained (labdha)
lines.en: At the feet of [Lūyī]{p-luyi}, [Dārika]{p-darika} has gained the [twelve stages]{dvadasa-bhumi}.

flags.note: Ten or twelve. The Bengali has dvādaśabhuaṇa, 'twelve worlds'; Munidatta reads 'having the twelve stages' (dvādaśabhūmino) (cp.34.m6); the Tibetan line has sa bcu, 'the ten stages', while the Tibetan comment has sa bcu gnyis pa, 'the twelve (or twelfth) stage(s)'. The Tibetan line has seven syllables (dA ri ka pas sa bcu thob), so gnyis may have been dropped for the metre, or the translators fell back on the bodhisattva's familiar ten. The draft follows the Bengali count.

The glossary's 'twelve stages' (dvadasa-bhumi) is used, as the rule requires, but bhuaṇa means 'world(s)', as in tiṇi bhuaṇa, 'the three worlds'; 'stages' is Munidatta's bhūmi (cp.34.m6). A literal line would read 'has gained the twelve worlds'. See questions.

luipāapae is taken as Lūipāa (Lūyīpāda, the name with its honorific) and pae, 'at the feet'; the English keeps the glossary's 'Lūyī'. The Tibetan adds 'by the kindness' (drin gyis) of his feet, as Munidatta has 'by the grace' (prasādāt) (cp.34.m6). The -em̐ of bhuaṇem̐ may be locative ('gained ... in the twelve worlds') rather than marking the object of ladhā.

notes.text: Rāga: a melodic mode of Indian music. Each song is headed by the rāga to which it is sung; this one is Varāḍī (Sanskrit music treatises name a rāga Varāṭī). The Tibetan heading transcribes the name, ba ra Di.

Shastri's heading gives only the rāga. The attribution dārikapādānām, 'of Dārikapāda', is written before the song; the edition prints it at the head of 1a, and it is not part of the verse. The Tibetan heading names both: 'the melody called Barāḍi, of Dārikapāda' (ba ra Di zhes bya ba'i glu dbyangs dA ri ka pa'i zhabs kyi'o).

The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) renders each long Bengali half-line as two short lines of seven syllables, so each couplet becomes four Tibetan lines. Words are sometimes moved between the short lines, added or dropped to fit them: see 1b, 2a, 2b, 4b and 5b.

Munidatta introduces the song as the siddha master Dārika setting out 'that same meaning' through realizing the profound dharma (cp.34.m1). Leaving out the refrain, he calls couplets 3, 4 and 5 the second, third and fourth verses: an address to another (cp.34.m4), praise of the path (cp.34.m5), and the poet's praise of himself (cp.34.m6). The Tibetan comment on couplet 4 says 'second verse' (rkang pa gnyis pas), apparently a slip.

Munidatta reads compassion as conventional truth and emptiness as its perfected form, ultimate truth; the line's nondifference is taking the two as non-different (abhedopacāra), which Dārika does by the vajra guru's grace. He backs this with a scripture verse: emptiness is nothing other than things, and there is no thing without it (cp.34.m2). Where the Sanskrit has conventional truth, the Tibetan comment has conventional bodhicitta (kun rdzob byang chub kyi sems).

bārem̐ is uncertain: perhaps the instrumental of a noun bāra, 'way, manner' (or 'turn, time'). Munidatta's abhedopacāreṇa, 'by treating as non-different' (cp.34.m2), and the Tibetan dbye ba med pas, 'by being undivided', both take the phrase as instrumental, which the draft's 'through' follows. kāabākcia (kāya-vāk-citta) has no case ending; the draft joins it to Dārika's play in 1b, as Munidatta does.

The image is of Dārika at play, at his ease, 'in the sky, on the far shore' (gaaṇata pārimakulem̐, two locatives side by side). The far shore is the further bank of a river, the goal of a crossing, a common Buddhist image; here it is set in the sky, and no river or boat is named.

Munidatta reads the sky as the three emptinesses beginning with light (ālokādiśūnyatraya) and its far shore as clear light (prabhāsvara), where Dārika plays with great bliss 'by the rule of the manifestation of purified body, speech and mind' (cp.34.m2). The Tibetan comment has the far shore 'wholly filled with great bliss' and the play 'with the certainty that body, speech and mind are free of intrinsic nature' (rang bzhin dang bral ba).

The Tibetan of 1b reads rnam par rol pa dA ri ka / pha rol mchog gi 'gram du song, 'Dārika, at play, went to the bank of the supreme far side'. It has no word for the sky, adds 'went' (song), which the Bengali lacks, and renders pārima, 'further', as pha rol mchog, 'the supreme far side', as if reading parama, 'supreme'.

The refrain's second line repeats 1b word for word (bilasai dārika gaaṇata pārimakulem̐), and the English repeats 1b exactly. Shastri's text already prints the refrain cue ধ্রু after 1b, perhaps because that line returns in the refrain; the cue is not translated.

The Tibetan does not repeat itself as the Bengali does. Its 2b reads dA ri ka pa nam mkha' la / pha rol mchog gi 'gram du song, 'Dārikapa, in the sky, went to the bank of the supreme far side': the sky is present and the play is missing, because the Tibetan has moved the play into 2a, bde ba chen pos rnam par rol, '(the mind) revels in great bliss'.

Munidatta says the refrain makes the same meaning firm. On alakha he comments that the mind, unmarkable, is marked by non-arising; then 'by that, in the clear-light mind, he does not play' (na vilasati), the rest being easy (cp.34.m3). The Tibetan comment has no negative: by that, with the clear-light mind, he plays and goes to the far side of bliss (rnam par rol par byed de bde ba'i pha rol du 'gro ba'o). The Sanskrit na may be corrupt.

Munidatta says that with this verse the poet addresses another, and supplies 'hey, lad, novice yogin' (re vaṭa bālayogin). He takes mantra as the muttering of outer mantras and tantra as reading the tantras, and paraphrases 3b: by the play of non-abiding great bliss your nirvāṇa, hard to discern, is accomplished by the grace of the rays of the dust of the guru's feet. He quotes Saraha: 'no mantra, no tantra' (cp.34.m4). The Tibetan comment says instead that the poet addresses 'not another' (gzhan ma yin par), and calls him a 'childish, deluded yogin' (byis pa rmongs pa'i rnal 'byor pa).

The Tibetan line reads khyod kyi sngags gang khyod rgyud dang / khyod kyi bsam gtan ci zhig bshad, 'what is your mantra, your tantra, and what concentration of yours do you explain?' Its 'your' with each item supports reading kinto as 'what to you'; it makes bakhāne a verb, 'explain' (bshad).

The song has līṇe, 'absorbed, dissolved' (Sanskrit līna); Munidatta's paraphrase has līlayā, 'by the play' (cp.34.m4). The Tibetan line (thim, 'dissolved') and the Tibetan comment (thim pa'i phyir, 'because of dissolving') agree with the song, and the draft follows it.

The Tibetan line reads rang gnas bde ba chen por thim / mtshon dka' don dam mya ngan 'das, 'dissolved in great bliss, one's own place; hard to indicate, the ultimate nirvāṇa'. rang gnas, 'own place', for apaiṭhāna, 'non-abiding', looks like a reading of apa as Old Bengali apā, 'self', and ṭhāna as 'place'; the Tibetan comment has rab tu mi gnas pa, 'non-abiding', matching Munidatta's apratiṣṭhāna (cp.34.m4). It renders parama, 'supreme', as don dam, 'ultimate'.

Munidatta calls this verse praise of the path. He glosses 'with suffering' as made one with ultimate truth, and turns the line into an instruction: 'O novice yogin, having asked the guru, enjoy the sense objects and senses' (viṣayendriyopabhoga). By this means Dārika, having gone to the unsurpassed of all, does not see in saṃsāra the division of self, other and the rest. He quotes a verse of Dhokaṛipāda in which the speaker, having examined everything in the pair of being and nonbeing with his own wisdom, sees no side that disputants proclaim (cp.34.m5). The Tibetan comment explains suffering as 'the happiness and suffering of saṃsāra'.

indījānī is filed under indrajāla, 'magic show' (literally 'Indra's net'; Old Bengali indiāla in song 30), and the Tibetan line's mig 'phrul dra ba, 'net of magic', supports this. The long ī and the final -ī are unexpected, so another word may lie behind the form. Munidatta does not cite the word; his paraphrase has the enjoyment of sense objects and senses in its place, as if hearing indriya, 'sense', in it, as he does with indiāla in song 30; the Tibetan comment agrees (yul dang dbang po nye bar longs spyod) (cp.34.m5). The line keeps the magic show.

A magic show (indrajāla) is a conjuror's display, a stock Indian image for appearances that seem real and are not. In the line someone makes suffering and happiness one and then enjoys, or eats (bhuñjai), the show.

The Tibetan line reads bde sdug gcig tu byas nas ni / mig 'phrul dra ba za bar byed, 'having made happiness and suffering one, eats the net of magic'. It puts happiness first (bde sdug) and takes bhuñjai as 'eats' (za ba).

svaparāpara is taken as sva, para and apara: self, other and not-other. The Tibetan line has rang gzhan gzhan nyid, 'self, other, otherness', and the Tibetan comment rang dang pha rol dang gzhan, 'self, the other side and another'; Munidatta repeats the compound with vibhāga and bheda, 'division, distinction' (cp.34.m5). saalānuttaramāṇī is perhaps sakala-anuttara-mānin, 'deeming all unsurpassed'; Munidatta paraphrases sakalānuttaraṃ gatvā, 'having gone to the unsurpassed of all' (cp.34.m5).

The Tibetan line has no negative: rang gzhan gzhan nyid dA ri ka / ma lus bla na med par shes, 'self, other, otherness: Dārika knows all, without remainder, as unsurpassed'. Where the Bengali has na cebai, 'does not perceive', and Munidatta na paśyati, 'does not see' (cp.34.m5), the Tibetan has only shes, 'knows', perhaps for cebai or for māṇī.

Munidatta calls this verse the poet's praise of himself. The three utterances 'king' point to his own qualities, lordship of the body and the rest; the others, gods, lords of nāgas and the like, stay bound by delusion about sense objects, while 'we', by Lūyīpāda's grace, having the twelve stages, are equal to the Jinas (cp.34.m6). The Tibetan comment has 'his own activity (bya ba), lordship and the other qualities', perhaps reading kārya for kāya.

The poet cries out 'king' three times and sets himself against other kings bound by delusion; the song does not say who the first king is. Tibetan lives of the eighty-four siddhas make Dārika a king who became Lūyī's disciple, a story the cries may play on.

The Tibetan line reads rgyal po rgyal po nyid kyi rgyal / gzhan yang rgyal po rmongs pas 'ching, 'king, king, king of [the king] himself; others too, kings, are bound by delusion'. Its third 'king' is a genitive phrase, as if reading rāāre as rāāra, 'of the king', not rāā with the vocative re.

Ten or twelve: the Bengali has dvādaśabhuaṇa, 'twelve worlds'; Munidatta reads twelve stages (dvādaśabhūmino) (cp.34.m6); the Tibetan line has sa bcu, 'the ten stages', while the Tibetan comment has sa bcu gnyis pa, 'the twelve (or twelfth) stage(s)'. The Tibetan line has seven syllables (dA ri ka pas sa bcu thob), so gnyis may have been dropped for the metre, or the translators fell back on the bodhisattva's familiar ten. The Tibetan line also adds 'by the kindness' (drin gyis) of Lūyīpa's feet, close to Munidatta's 'by the grace' (prasādāt).

bhuaṇa is bhuvana, 'world', as in tiṇi bhuaṇa, 'the three worlds'; 'stages' (bhūmi) is Munidatta's reading (cp.34.m6), which the glossary's 'twelve stages' follows. The ending -em̐ of bhuaṇem̐ may be locative ('gained ... in the twelve worlds'). luipāapae is taken as Lūipāa, Lūyīpāda with his honorific, and pae, 'at the feet'; ladhā is labdha, 'gained'.

termsOmitted.reason: pārimakulem̐ is rendered as one phrase, 'far shore', marked with para (whose listed variant it is); marking 'shore' separately would split the phrase.
As in 1b: 'far shore' renders pārima-kula together and is marked with para.

proposals.definition: Exposition or explanation (Sanskrit vyākhyāna, Old Bengali bakhāna): expounding a text or practice in words, the work of scholars and teachers. Song 34 (3a) asks what use concentration and exposition are; Munidatta has dhyānavyākhyāna (cp.34.m4), and the Tibetan line makes it a verb, bshad, 'explain'.
proposals.rationale: A scholastic activity the siddhas set against realization, named in 3a beside mantra, tantra and concentration, which all have entries; marking it lets the reader see the list as a list. Whether the word recurs in other songs is unchecked. Tibetan bshad is too common to match on, so only the Bengali and Sanskrit forms are given for matching.

questions: 3a jhāṇa: the draft uses the glossary's 'concentration' (dhyana), keeping 'meditation' for bhāvanā. In this line, beside mantra, tantra and exposition, 'meditation' would read more naturally. Keep 'concentration', or allow 'meditation' for dhyāna in contexts like this one (which would blur the two entries)?

4a indījānī: the draft keeps 'magic show' (indrajala), which the Tibetan line supports (mig 'phrul dra ba). Munidatta's paraphrase has the enjoyment of sense objects and senses instead (cp.34.m5). Do you accept 'magic show' despite the odd form indījānī? Should indījānī stay among indrajala's forms with a note on the form, or be kept in source form until it is explained?

5b: the glossary's 'twelve stages' follows Munidatta's dvādaśabhūmi (cp.34.m6), but the Bengali says dvādaśa bhuaṇa, 'twelve worlds', and the Tibetan line 'ten stages'. Should the line say 'twelve worlds' and leave the stages to the note? That would need a variant or a separate entry for dvadasa-bhumi.

p-darika's approved English is 'Dārikapāda', but the poet calls himself Dārika (1b, 2b, 4b, 5b). The draft writes [Dārika]{p-darika} to keep his self-naming. Could 'Dārika' be added as a listed variant, as 'Bhusuku' is for Bhusukupāda?

4b: is 'self and other, or not-other' acceptable for svaparāpara, and 'he deems all unsurpassed' for saalānuttaramāṇī? Alternatives: 'self, other and another'; 'deeming himself unsurpassed among all'; or, with Munidatta, 'having gone to the unsurpassed of all' (cp.34.m5).

3b: the draft sets the halves side by side ('Absorbed in non-abiding great bliss: supreme nirvāṇa, hard to discern'). Would you prefer the locative reading ('... in supreme nirvāṇa, hard to discern') or Munidatta's construction, with nirvāṇa as what the absorption accomplishes (cp.34.m4)?
1a: bārem̐ is rendered 'through' ('Through the nondifference of emptiness and compassion'). Do you know a better-attested sense of bāra that fits here?

Heading: the input heading has only the rāga, so the draft gives 'Rāga Varāḍī' without the poet; the attribution dārikapādānām stands before the song. Should the heading read 'Rāga Varāḍī · Dārikapāda', like the model heading in the brief?
The particle re is 'hey' in 3a and 'O' in 5a ('O king'). Keep the two, or use one rendering throughout?
The proposal vyakhyana ('exposition') marks bakhāne in 3a. Is it worth an entry, or should 'exposition' stay unmarked?
